title: Rare Trades
description: Ten profiles of people in uncommon trades: a bell founder, a thatcher, a wheelwright, a piano tuner, a museum taxidermist, a bookbinder, a stained-glass restorer, a cooper, a lighthouse lens keeper and a fountain pen maker.

lessons.title: The Bell Founder
lessons.summary: A bell founder casts and tunes a new bell for a convent, carrying the date of the truce of 1918.
lessons.text:
Ruth Hallam has been casting bells for forty years, and she still speaks of each one as if it had a voice of its own.

Every bell begins as a mold. Ruth builds the inner part, the core, from clay mixed with sand, straw and goat hair, which holds the clay together as it dries. Over the core she shapes a false bell of clay, exactly as thick as the finished metal will be, and over that she builds the outer mold. When the false bell is broken away and the mold is closed again, an empty space is left in the shape of a bell.

Most bells carry decoration near the top, and Ruth's favorite is a garland of oak leaves. She shapes each garland in wax and fixes it to the false bell, so that it leaves its print inside the outer mold. Beneath the garland goes the inscription.

On the day of the casting, bronze, roughly four parts copper to one part tin, is heated until it glows like a setting sun and is poured into the buried mold in a single steady stream. A large bell may need a week to cool.

A bell does not sound one note but several simultaneous notes: a deep hum, a main note and a family of higher tones, all of which must agree with one another. Ruth turns the bell upside down on a slow turning machine and shaves thin rings of metal from the inside; metal taken from each height changes a different tone. Because nothing can be put back, she works in tiny steps and records each measurement in her own notation, a private system of numbers and arrows. Only her assistant can read that notation. A poorly tuned bell sounds sour, as if its simultaneous voices were arguing. A well-tuned bell sounds distinctly sweet, and each of its tones can be heard distinctly, even across a valley.

This spring she is finishing a bell for a convent in the hills. The old bell of the convent cracked last winter after more than a century of service. In 1918, the sisters say, it rang for an hour when news of the truce that ended the war reached the valley, and the sisters have asked Ruth to cast the date of the truce beneath the garland.

The blessing of the new bell will be televised by a local station. Ruth, who dislikes cameras, has seen her bells televised before and always stands at the back. With the ceremony impending, she sleeps badly and checks her numbers once more. Yet the impending day also pleases her. A bell, she likes to say, will speak for three hundred years, and she only gives it its first breath.

Questions:
How does the garland of oak leaves get onto a bell?
Ruth shapes it in wax and fixes it to the false bell, so that it leaves its print inside the outer mold.
How does Ruth tune a bell?
She turns it upside down on a slow turning machine and shaves thin rings of metal from the inside.
Why does she work in tiny steps and record everything in her notation?
She works slowly because metal that has been removed cannot be put back.
Why will the new bell carry the date of the truce of 1918?
The old bell of the convent rang for an hour when news of that truce reached the valley.

lessons.title: A Roof of Reed
lessons.summary: A thatcher explains how a reed roof is cut, laid and protected, and takes his lunch on a cottage doorstep.
lessons.text:
Owen Hext is a thatcher, one of a few hundred left in England, and he spends his days on ladders above the villages of Devon. A thatcher must be a good climber, and Owen calls himself a climber who has never climbed anything taller than a cottage. He says it in an upbeat voice, and his upbeat mood survives even February rain.

His material is water reed. It grows in wide wet beds near the coast, and it is cut in winter, after the leaves have fallen and the stems have turned the color of honey. In his youth Owen helped the reed cutters mow the beds by hand; today most of the reed is mowed by machine, then tied in bundles and stacked to dry.

On the roof, the work begins at the bottom edge and rises in rows. Owen lays each bundle with its cut ends facing out, fixes it to the wooden frame of the roof with steel hooks or twisted pins of hazel, and beats the ends into place with a flat wooden tool whose face is cut with grooves. Each blow pushes the reed a little higher, until the surface is as tight and even as the fur of an animal. Done well, a reed roof will keep a house dry for fifty years.

The work is hard on the hands. Every new apprentice gets a blister in the first week, then another blister beneath the first. Owen's own palms are as tough as leather.

Old roofs bring their own problems. A neglected roof can be overrun with moss, which holds water and rots the reed from above; last year Owen stripped a roof so overrun that small plants were growing from it. Sparrows and mice love the warm reed, and they are sneaky about it, starting their tunnels on the side of the roof that nobody looks at. Owen covers a finished roof with fine wire net, which keeps out even the most sneaky visitor.

Not every roof is reed. In the hills of the north, people once used ling, the low purple heather that covers the moors. A ling roof was heavier and darker, and Owen has repaired only two in his life.

At noon he eats his lunch on the doorstep of whatever cottage he is working on, with a small radio beside him. If there is a soccer matchup that afternoon, he follows it closely. Last spring he and an owner sat on her doorstep and argued happily about a matchup for an hour. Then he went back up the ladder, because the roof would not finish itself.

Questions:
How is the reed for Owen's roofs harvested?
It is cut in winter; it was once mowed by hand, and today most of it is mowed by machine and tied in bundles.
What happens to the hands of a new apprentice?
Every new apprentice gets a blister in the first week, and then another blister beneath the first.
Why does Owen cover a finished roof with wire net?
Sparrows and mice are sneaky about making tunnels in the reed, and the net keeps them out.
Where does Owen eat his lunch?
He eats it on the doorstep of the cottage he is working on, beside a small radio.

lessons.title: The Wheel Maker
lessons.summary: A Missouri wheelwright builds and repairs wooden wheels the way they were made for the wagons of the West.
lessons.text:
In a barn outside a small town in Missouri, Isaac Lowry makes wooden wheels the way they were made when westbound wagons left the river towns for the long road to Oregon. Missouri was once the last outpost of settled country, and every westbound family that left such an outpost depended on its wheels, and on men like Isaac's great-grandfather, who built them.

A wooden wheel is three woods working together. The hub, at the center, is a thick block that must not split. The spokes, usually of oak, carry the weight. The rim is built from curved sections of ash, a wood that bends without breaking. Isaac cuts the joints by hand, with blades he hones every morning on a flat stone. A blade that has not been honed, he says, tears the wood instead of cutting it.

Few people notice that a good wheel is not flat. It is shaped like a very shallow cone, with the spokes leaning slightly outward. This shape, called dish, lets the wheel take the sideways shocks of a rough road.

At the end, Isaac heats an iron tire in a ring of fire until it glows, lifts it with long tongs and drops it over the wooden wheel. His helpers pour cold water over it at once. The iron shrinks as it cools, steam rises in clouds, and the whole wheel is squeezed so tightly that every joint closes. Visitors are always amused by the noise and steam, and they are just as amused by Isaac, who talks to the wheel the whole time.

Most of his work today is repair. Museums send him carriages with loose wheels, and farmers bring old wagons from their barns. Last month a historical society brought a wagon with two spokes severed in a fall from a truck; the rim had cracked where the severed spokes met it. Isaac judged the old wheel unfit for the road but good enough for display, and he built a new one for the wagon. A loose or cracked wheel, he explains, is unfit for any journey.

He keeps finished wheels on a low trolley that he rolls from bench to bench, and his grandchildren like to ride the trolley when he is not looking.

Isaac is not hostile to modern machines. He has read about robotics, and he once visited a factory where robotics did almost all of the work. Still, he believes that some knowledge lives in the hands, and that a wheel made by hand teaches its maker something that no machine can learn for him.

Questions:
Why did westbound families depend on men like Isaac's great-grandfather?
They depended on their wheels, and those men built and repaired the wheels.
Why does Isaac hone his blades every morning?
A blade that has not been honed tears the wood instead of cutting it.
Why is a good wheel shaped like a shallow cone?
The shape, called dish, lets the wheel take the sideways shocks of a rough road.
What happens when the hot iron tire is cooled with water?
The iron shrinks, steam rises, and the wheel is squeezed so tightly that every joint closes.
What did Isaac decide about the wagon with two severed spokes?
He judged the old wheel unfit for the road but good enough for display, and he built a new one.

lessons.title: Before the Concert
lessons.summary: A piano tuner prepares a concert grand in an empty hall and listens to the evening's first notes.
lessons.text:
Two hours before a concert, the auditorium of the city's music hall is dark except for a single light above the stage, and Nora Castell is alone with the piano. She tunes pianos for a living, and on concert days she tunes this one for the evening's pianist. The empty auditorium is so quiet that she can hear the building settle.

A concert grand has about 230 strings, and together they pull on its iron frame with a force of roughly twenty tons. Most notes have three strings, which must sound exactly alike. Nora silences two of them with a strip of felt, tunes the third, and then lets the others speak one at a time. When two strings are close to the same pitch but not quite there, she hears a slow beat in the sound, a soft pulse like a ripple on still water. As she turns the pin with her tuning lever, the beat slows, and when it stops, the two strings sound as one.

Scientists say that sound is processed in the temporal lobe, a region on each side of the brain, just above the ears. Nora likes to joke that her left lobe works harder than her right. Whatever the cause, years of practice have trained her to hear differences that most listeners would consider insignificant, far smaller than the step between two keys. To her, nothing in a piano is insignificant.

She does not fret about the clock, though the clock is always there. Fretting, she has found, makes her hands tense and her ears less sharp. Instead she sits still on the bench for a minute before she starts and breathes slowly. A friend taught her to meditate years ago, and she now meditates in empty halls more often than anywhere else.

Tonight the pianist is accompanying a singer, an alto with a warm, dark voice. During the last hour the two of them practice while Nora waits at the side of the stage, and she cannot help but overhear them. She overhears the alto ask for one song to be taken more slowly, and she hears the pianist laugh and agree.

Then the hall fills. For Nora the opening minutes of a concert are full of suspense; she listens to the first chords the way a builder watches the first truck cross a new bridge. The suspense fades once she hears that the high notes are holding.

During the break she walks onto the stage with her lever and checks a few notes while the audience talks. The pianist, passing, tells her that the instrument feels marvelous. Nora thanks her, though she knows that the marvelous part belongs to the people who built it. Her job is only to remove the small faults that would stand between the music and the room.

Questions:
How does she know when two strings are in tune?
The slow beat in the sound stops, and the two strings sound as one.
What part of the brain processes sound, according to scientists?
The temporal lobe, a region on each side of the brain, just above the ears, processes sound.
What does Nora do instead of fretting about the clock?
She sits still on the bench, breathes slowly and meditates for a minute before she starts.
What does Nora overhear while she waits?
She overhears the alto ask for one song to be taken more slowly, and the pianist agree.

lessons.title: The Fox Under the Birches
lessons.summary: A museum taxidermist explains where her animals come from and how she prepared a fox for a winter scene.
lessons.text:
Visitors to the hall of local fauna at the city's natural history museum rarely think about the person who arranged the animals. For twenty years that person has been Miriam Holt, the museum's taxidermist. If visitors believe for a moment that the fox is alive, she has done her job.

None of the animals in the hall were killed for display. They come from zoos, from wildlife hospitals and from the side of the road, and each one is a scientific record before it is an exhibit. Before Miriam begins, a museum biologist takes small samples, a little muscle and sometimes the thyroid, and stores them in a freezer for future research. A thyroid kept today might help a scientist, fifty years from now, understand how the bodies of wild animals responded to a changing world. The museum's fauna, in other words, is also a library.

Modern work of this kind has little to do with stuffing. Miriam preserves the skin and fits it over a body she has carved from foam. She sets glass eyes and shapes the small details of the face with clay. The hardest part is posture. A fox is a patient stalker of mice, and she wanted hers to look like a stalker: low to the ground, ears forward, every muscle ready. She studied films for weeks until the crouch was right, the body crouched so low that its belly almost touches the snow.

The fox now stands in a winter scene beneath a group of birch trees. The birch trunks are real, gathered after a storm, and their white bark glows under the lights. Miriam liked the idea of a fox moving with stealth through a pale forest; stealth, she says, is the whole character of that animal. Lurking at the edge of the scene, half hidden, is an owl, and many children only find the owl lurking there on their second visit.

Further along the hall, a family of otters shows the playful side of nature. They slide down a bank of artificial mud, and one holds a stone between its paws, as playful otters really do.

Miriam is less fond of some older work. In the museum's back rooms are pieces from more than a century ago in which squirrels wear tiny hats and sit at card tables. She finds them a little vulgar, though she understands their charm. A vulgar joke, she says, can be forgiven; the real fault is to show an animal doing something it never does.

For a child, the hall is a kind of wonderland, a place where wild animals stand still long enough to be studied. Miriam remembers it as her own wonderland when she was eight, and that memory still brings her to work each morning.

Questions:
Why does a biologist take samples such as the thyroid?
The samples are stored for future research, so that scientists can understand how wild animals responded to a changing world.
How did Miriam make the fox look like a stalker?
She studied films for weeks until its crouch was right, low to the ground with its ears forward.
What is lurking at the edge of the winter scene?
An owl is lurking there, half hidden, and many children only find it on their second visit.
What does Miriam think of the old pieces with squirrels in tiny hats?
She finds them a little vulgar, though she understands their charm.

lessons.title: The Book Doctor
lessons.summary: A bookbinder cleans, repairs and resews a merchant's old memorandum book and teaches evening classes.
lessons.text:
Thomas Reyes repairs books in a narrow room above a hardware store, and the first thing he does with any old book is hold one of its pages up to the window. Seen against the light, a sheet of handmade paper often shows a watermark, a faint picture or name formed in the paper while it was still wet. The watermark can tell him where the paper came from and roughly when it was made.

The second thing he does is clean it. Old pages carry the grime of centuries: smoke from oil lamps, the oil of many thumbs, dust that has settled into every fold. Thomas does not use water. He sprinkles soft eraser crumbs over a page and moves them gently in small circles with his fingertips. The crumbs lift the grime and roll it away, and he brushes them off into a tray. A page cleaned this way looks brighter but not new, as he wants.

This week his bench holds a merchant's memorandum book from a river port, in which a trader recorded debts, prices and the weather. The memorandum book had been rebound once, badly, and the earlier binder had omitted a whole section of pages, which Thomas found loose at the back. He will sew the omitted pages back into their proper place on cords of linen thread.

Wheat paste, which he cooks himself, is bland in smell and color, and that bland quality is a virtue: it will not stain the paper. For the spine he uses animal glue, made from skin and bone. Chemically, it is a tangle of protein chains called peptides. When it is warmed, each peptide chain loosens and the glue flows; as it cools, the chains knot together again and hold. Because warmth can soften it, a future binder will be able to undo his work.

For the finest repairs he keeps a few sheets of an unusual material made from the thin outer layer of cattle intestine. It was once used for beating gold into leaf, and it is still prized for mending tears in old pages, since a strip of intestine is thinner than paper yet very strong.

Next to the memorandum book lies a student's paperback novel about undead creatures who rise from their graves, its cover hanging by a thread. The student loves it, so Thomas will mend the undead as carefully as the merchant.

When he first offered evening classes in simple binding, there were few takers. Now every class fills, and the takers include nurses, lawyers and retired teachers, all eager to make one book with their own hands.

Questions:
What can a watermark tell Thomas?
It can tell him where the paper came from and roughly when it was made.
How does Thomas clean the grime from old pages?
He sprinkles soft eraser crumbs over a page, moves them in small circles and brushes them away.
What had the earlier binder done wrong with the memorandum book?
The earlier binder had omitted a whole section of pages, which Thomas found loose at the back.
Why is animal glue useful for a book's spine?
Its peptide chains loosen when it is warmed, so a future binder will be able to undo the work.
Why is the material made from cattle intestine good for mending tears?
It is thinner than paper yet very strong.

lessons.title: The Window of the Giant
lessons.summary: A stained-glass restorer saves a church window given by families who had fled the turmoil of war.
lessons.text:
Marta Novak learned her trade in Prague, where she spent her twenties among a bohemian crowd of painters and musicians, painting glass at night. Bohemia has been famous for its glass for centuries, and she still orders certain colors from a small Bohemian workshop that makes them by the same recipes it used in her grandmother's time. Today she restores stained glass in a workshop in Chicago.

A stained glass window is a puzzle of colored pieces held in strips of lead with a groove along each side. Where the strips meet, they are joined with melted metal, and a dark paste is pushed beneath the lead to keep out the rain. The colors are in the glass itself; faces and hands are painted on in a brown paint that is fired until it becomes part of the surface.

The word plumber comes from the old Roman word for lead, and centuries ago a plumber was simply a worker in lead, laying roofs and pipes, while the window makers prepared their own strips nearby.

Lead does not last forever. After about a century it grows tired, and a window begins to bend between its iron bars. When Marta was called to a church on the north side of the city, its great east window was on the brink of collapse; one panel had pulled so far from its frame that daylight showed around it. A window on the brink, she says, can fall in a single storm.

She took the window down panel by panel and carried the panels to her workshop. She saves every piece of original glass she can, joining cracks with a clear glue rather than cutting new pieces. Where a piece is missing, she makes a replacement and marks its edge, so that no one who works on it later will mistake her fabrication for the original. Honest fabrication, she believes, is part of the craft.

The window has a history of its own. It was paid for in 1946 by families who had come to the city after the turmoil of the war, many of them escaping tyranny and repression at home. They chose an old story for it: David and Goliath. In the central panel, the giant stands in armor with a curved saber at his side, and he opens his mouth to taunt the young shepherd. The saber is a single long piece of pale yellow glass. A painted scroll repeats the giant's taunt in old letters. Beneath it, the families added a line of their own, thanking the city that had sheltered them from tyranny.

Those families had known repression and turmoil, and they gave their new city a window full of light.

Questions:
What did the word plumber mean centuries ago?
A plumber was simply a worker in lead, who laid roofs and pipes.
Why did the church window need to be taken down?
The old lead had grown tired, and the window was on the brink of collapse.
Why does Marta mark the edge of each new piece she makes?
She marks it so that no one who works on it later will mistake her fabrication for the original glass.
Who paid for the window, and what does its central panel show?
Families who had escaped tyranny and repression paid for it, and it shows Goliath with a saber, about to taunt the young shepherd David.

lessons.title: The Barrel Maker
lessons.summary: A Kentucky cooper raises, bends and chars oak barrels for bourbon and brandy without glue or nails.
lessons.text:
Visitors hear Frank Doyle's workshop before they see it. The racket of steel on oak, the ring of hammers driving metal bands down the sides of barrels, can be heard from the parking lot, and inside, the racket is so loud that the workers wear ear protection. Frank is a cooper, a maker of barrels, in the hills of Kentucky, and his customers are the companies that make bourbon and, more and more often, small makers of brandy.

A barrel holds liquid without a drop of glue or a single nail. It is made of about thirty narrow boards of white oak, called staves, each one wider in the middle than at the ends and cut at a slight angle along its edges. The cooper stands the staves upright inside a steel band, like the petals of a closed flower, while their loose ends spread open below. To bend them together, he sets the barrel over a small fire of oak shavings, softens the wood with heat and steam, and slowly pulls the open end closed with a cable. Then he drives more bands down over the curved sides until the staves press against one another so hard that they seal.

For bourbon, the inside is then burned until it is black, because the law requires bourbon to age in new charred oak. For brandy, many makers prefer the wood only lightly toasted, so that the brandy tastes gently sweet rather than smoky.

In the old tradition of the trade, it is customary, at the end of an apprenticeship of about four years, for a new cooper to be rolled across the floor inside a barrel covered in shavings, water and flour, while the whole shop bangs on the wood. Afterward, as is customary, he is lifted out and welcomed as an equal.

Frank's attire never changes: a denim shirt, denim trousers and a heavy leather apron, the same work attire his father wore. His hands show the trade. They are thick, scarred and stained by oak, and a manicure, he says, would last about ten minutes in his shop. The manicure his daughter gave him before her wedding lasted only until the next morning.

The workload rises and falls with the market. When bourbon sells well, the workload doubles, and the shop runs from dawn to dark.

He is a quiet man, and his plain honesty tends to disarm visitors who expect a salesman. Asked whether a machine could do his job, he answers that machines already do half of it, and that the other half is listening. Then he taps a finished barrel with his knuckle. A barrel that rings clearly is a sound barrel, he says, and the simplicity of that test disarms even the most cautious buyer.

Questions:
How does a cooper bend the staves of a barrel together?
He sets the barrel over a small fire of oak shavings, softens the wood with heat and steam, and pulls the open end closed with a cable.
Why is the inside of a bourbon barrel burned black?
The law requires bourbon to age in new charred oak.
What is customary at the end of a cooper's apprenticeship?
The new cooper is rolled across the floor inside a barrel covered in shavings, water and flour, and then welcomed as an equal.
What is Frank's work attire?
He wears a denim shirt, denim trousers and a heavy leather apron.

lessons.title: The Keeper of the Lens
lessons.summary: A woman cares for the old glass lens of a lighthouse that now runs on solar power.
lessons.text:
Hannah Lind looks after a single object: the great lens of a lighthouse on the coast of Maine that is now a museum. The light has run automatically for decades, but the old lens still stands in the glass room at the top of the tower, and Hannah climbs the 96 steps twice a week to care for it.

The lens follows the design of the French engineer Augustin Fresnel, who in 1822 solved an old problem. A flame gives off light in every direction, and most of that light is wasted on the sky. Fresnel surrounded the flame with rings of glass, each ring cut at a precise angle, so that together they bent the scattered light into a single flat beam aimed at the horizon. Hannah's lens, set in a brass frame, is taller than she is.

Fresnel was also a scientist of light itself. Like many people of his time, he believed that light traveled as a wave through the ether, an invisible substance that was thought to fill all of space. Physics later abandoned the idea of the ether, but the lenses built on his calculations still work perfectly.

Standing inside the lens on a sunny day is like standing inside a small cosmos: every surface throws back a spark, and the walls are full of rainbows. Hannah says that this cosmos of glass is the reason she took the job.

The history of the tower is plainer. The keepers lived in a small house at its foot with few amenities: no running water until 1931, a stove and a narrow bunk for whoever had the night watch. The bunk is still there, and visitors are surprised by how few amenities a keeper had. In thick fog, before horns were installed, the station fired a gun at fixed intervals, and on bad nights the gunfire went on until morning. Sailors who could not see the light steered by the sound of the gunfire.

Sea charts give the light's position in latitude and longitude, and a captain unsure of his longitude could once check it against the light. During the war the light was kept dark, so that no enemy warship could use it, and a navy warship guarded the bay instead.

The old keepers could not foresee the modern station. Today a photovoltaic panel on the roof charges a battery, and that photovoltaic power runs a lamp brighter than the old flame. No keeper could have foreseen it, and none of them, Hannah believes, would have objected.

She polishes the glass with soft cloths and wears a linen apron, as the keepers did, so that no button scratches the glass. The lens has a timeless quality. Its working life is over, yet its timeless shape still seems to be looking out to sea.

Questions:
What problem did Augustin Fresnel solve?
A flame gives off light in every direction, and he bent the scattered light into a single flat beam aimed at the horizon.
What amenities did the keepers have?
They had very few amenities: no running water until 1931, a stove and a narrow bunk for the night watch.
How did sailors find their way in thick fog before horns were installed?
The station fired a gun at fixed intervals, and the sailors steered by the sound of the gunfire.
What powers the modern lamp?
A photovoltaic panel on the roof charges a battery, and that power runs the lamp.

lessons.title: The Pen Maker
lessons.summary: A fountain pen maker repairs pens of sentimental value, answers skeptics and teaches children to write by hand.
lessons.text:
Most of the people who write to Kenji Arai begin with a story. A grandmother's pen that has not written in fifty years, a father's pen found in a drawer: the objects arrive in padded envelopes with letters explaining why they matter. Kenji, who makes and repairs fountain pens in a small workshop in Portland, Oregon, has learned to read the letter before he opens the pen. The value of such a pen is mostly sentimental, and sentimental value, he believes, deserves the same care as money.

A fountain pen is a quiet piece of engineering. Under the gold point lies a strip of hard black rubber called the feed, cut with a channel no wider than a hair. Ink runs down the channel toward the point while air travels up it into the body of the pen, one replacing the other drop by drop. With too little air the pen stops; with too much ink it floods. The first fountain pens, made more than 140 years ago, were unreliable, leaking in pockets and dropping spots of ink on letters, and the history of the trade is largely the story of making them less unreliable.

The point is split down the middle by a fine slit, and its tip is a tiny ball of very hard metal, which Kenji shapes on fine stones until it glides across the paper. He hones each tip by hand and tests it between strokes, because a difference of a hair's width changes how a pen feels. Some customers want a pen that writes wet and broad; conversely, others want a fine, dry line for small handwriting.

Kenji meets a good deal of skepticism. People tell him that fountain pens are a regression, a step backward in a world of keyboards, passwords and logins. He understands the skepticism. He types all day himself, and every morning his login screen asks him to prove that he is not a robot. Yet he does not see writing by hand as a regression. Typing is fast; conversely, a pen is slow, and he believes that when the hand slows down, thoughts have time to arrange themselves.

Twice a year he offers a small batch of new pens on his website, and they sell within minutes. Customers sit at their screens and reload the page again and again, waiting for the button to appear. One woman told him that she had to reload eleven times.

On Thursday afternoons he visits a local middle school, where he teaches handwriting in an enrichment program. The enrichment classes are optional, but they are always full. The students fill their pens from bottles of blue ink, stain their fingers and leave delighted.

Questions:
Why does Kenji read the letter before he opens a pen?
The value of such a pen is mostly sentimental, and he believes sentimental value deserves the same care as money.
What does the feed of a fountain pen do?
It lets ink run down a narrow channel toward the point while air travels up into the body of the pen.
Why were the first fountain pens unreliable?
They leaked in pockets and dropped spots of ink on letters.
Why do some people treat fountain pens with skepticism?
They think fountain pens are a regression, a step backward in a world of keyboards, passwords and logins.
What do Kenji's students do in the enrichment program?
They fill their pens from bottles of blue ink, practice handwriting and leave delighted.
